description: Binary Search is an efficient algorithm for finding an item from a sorted list of items or a monotonic search space. It works by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. If the value of the search key is less than the item in the middle of the interval, narrow the interval to the lower half. Otherwise, narrow it to the upper half.
important_details: Precondition: The search space must be sorted or exhibit a monotonic property (a clear true/false boundary).
Time Complexity: O(log N), where N is the size of the search space.
Overflow Prevention: Calculate mid as `left + (right - left) / 2` instead of `(left + right) / 2` to prevent integer overflow.

Boundary Conditions: Choosing `left <= right` vs `left < right` and updating `left = mid + 1` vs `left = mid` is critical and depends on whether you are searching for an exact match or a boundary (lower/upper bound).
other_relevant_details: Binary search is not limited to searching in arrays. It can be applied to any function f(x) that is monotonic. If a problem asks to 'minimize the maximum' or 'maximize the minimum', it is often a binary search on the answer space.

variations.description: The standard binary search to find an exact match of a target value in a sorted array.
important_details: Loop condition is `left <= right` because the target might be at the exact `mid` index.
Return `mid` immediately when `nums[mid] == target`.
If target is greater, discard left half: `left = mid + 1`. If smaller, discard right half: `right = mid - 1`.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log N). Space Complexity: O(1).

problems.name: Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix
Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target

variations.description: Finding the first element that is >= target (lower bound) or > target (upper bound). Used when target might not exist exactly or we need insertion points.
important_details: Loop condition is `left < right` because we exit when the search space is narrowed to one element.
Do not return early when `nums[mid] == target`; keep searching left for the first occurrence (lower bound).
Update `right = mid` (not `mid - 1`) to avoid skipping the boundary element.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log N). Note the right initialization is `nums.length` (not `nums.length - 1`) to handle cases where the target is greater than all elements.

problems.name: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array

variations.description: Applying binary search to a range of possible answers (e.g., 1 to 10^14) rather than an array. We check if a given answer `mid` is feasible.
important_details: The search space must be monotonic (if `x` is possible, then any `y > x` is also possible, or vice versa).
Requires a helper function `isFeasible(mid)` that checks if a given answer satisfies the problem's constraints.
Find the transition point between impossible and possible answers.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log(Range) * Complexity of isFeasible). Often combined with greedy algorithms inside the feasibility check.

variations.variation: Binary Search on Rotated / Modified Array
variations.description: Searching in a sorted array that has been rotated or has a distinct peak (mountain). Requires identifying which half is sorted to make the next decision.
important_details: At least one half of the array (left or right of `mid`) will always be strictly sorted.
First, check if the left half is sorted (`nums[left] <= nums[mid]`). If yes, check if the target lies within it; otherwise, search the right half.
If the right half is sorted, check if the target lies within it; otherwise, search the left half.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log N). For arrays with duplicates (e.g., Rotated Sorted Array II), worst-case becomes O(N) because `nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right]` forces linear scanning.

variations.description: Searching in a 2D matrix where rows and columns are sorted, or the whole matrix can be treated as a 1D sorted array.
important_details: If the matrix is strictly sorted (M[i][n-1] < M[i+1][0]), treat it as a 1D array using `mid / n` and `mid % n` for row and column mapping.
If rows and columns are independently sorted, start at the top-right corner. If target is greater, move down; if smaller, move left.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(M + N) for step-wise search, O(log(M * N)) for 1D flattened search. Space: O(1).

Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix

variations.description: Combining binary search with prefix sums to answer range queries or subarray sum conditions efficiently.
important_details: Prefix sum array `prefix[i]` stores sum of first `i` elements. Sum of subarray `[L, R]` is `prefix[R+1] - prefix[L]`.
Used to optimize sliding window or subarray sum checks to O(1) inside the binary search feasibility function.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(N log N). Used to optimize two-pointer problems where sliding window isn't directly applicable due to negative numbers.

problems.name: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K

variations.description: Using a greedy approach to verify if a specific answer `mid` (e.g., minimum capacity, maximum distance) is feasible.
important_details: The feasibility function simulates the process with the given constraint `mid`.
If feasible, we try to optimize (minimize or maximize the answer) by adjusting the binary search bounds.
Greedy checks often involve iterating through the array and accumulating counts/sums.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(N log(Sum - Max)). Very common in OA and placement tests.

variations.description: Using binary search on the answer while a two-pointer approach validates the feasibility. Often used to find K-th smallest pairs or sums.
important_details: Binary search defines a target sum/distance.
Two pointers count how many pairs have a sum/distance <= target.
If count < K, increase binary search `low`; else decrease `high`.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(N log N + N log W) where W is the max distance. Combines sorting, BS, and Sliding Window.

problems.name: Kth Smallest Number in Multiplication Table
Kth Largest Element in an Array

variations.description: Using binary search over a sorted array or coordinate-compressed values, with a BIT or Segment Tree to dynamically maintain frequencies or counts of elements seen so far.
important_details: Often used for inversion counts or finding smaller elements after self.
Coordinate compression is usually required because values can be large, while BIT requires O(N) space.
Iterate from right to left. Query BIT for count of elements < current element. Update BIT with the current element.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(N log N). Segment Trees can also be used for range queries if dynamic updates are needed.

problems.name: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

variations.description: Using a min-heap or max-heap to find the K-th smallest/largest element among multiple sorted arrays or lists.
important_details: Push the first element of each sorted list into a min-heap.
Pop the minimum element and push the next element from the same list.
Repeat K times. The K-th popped element is the answer.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(K log N). Alternative to BS on Answer Space which takes O(N log(Range)).

variations.description: Finding a path in a graph where a certain parameter (e.g., maximum edge weight, minimum effort) is minimized. Binary search defines the threshold, and BFS checks connectivity.
important_details: Binary search on the possible range of weights/efforts.
BFS/DFS is used to check if the destination is reachable using only edges with weight <= mid.
If reachable, try to minimize the threshold; else increase it.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(M * N * log(Max Weight)). Alternative is Dijkstra's algorithm.

variations.description: Optimizing Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) from O(N^2) to O(N log N) using binary search.
important_details: Maintain an array `tails` where `tails[i]` stores the smallest tail of all increasing subsequences of length `i+1`.
For each element, use binary search to find its position in `tails`.
If it's larger than all elements, append it. Otherwise, replace the first element that is >= to it.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(N log N). Space: O(N). This does not directly reconstruct the sequence but only gives the length.

variations.description: Finding the maximum XOR of two numbers in an array by inserting elements into a Trie bit by bit and querying the opposite bit for maximization.
important_details: Insert binary representation of numbers (up to 32 bits) into a Trie.
For each number, traverse the Trie greedily choosing the opposite bit (1 if current bit is 0, else 0) to maximize XOR.
If the opposite bit doesn't exist, follow the same bit.

variations.description: Using binary search to find the maximum/minimum edge weight in a graph such that certain connectivity criteria (e.g., MST weight, number of components) are met.
important_details: Sort edges by weight.
Binary search on the edge weight threshold.
Use DSU to union edges <= threshold and check if components are connected or count is correct.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(E log E). Usually standard Kruskal's is sufficient, but BS+DSU helps when looking for a specific threshold.
